$$
{y}^{″}-5{y}^{′}+6y={e}^{7x}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{3x}.$ 

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

where $u_1 = u_1(x), u_2 = u_2(x),$ that satisfies the constraint
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/f6f630f08ab3b335d43d12fa90c45df8fad0c73b83df793f43958e1ada7d199c.png)

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating $u_1'$ and $u_2'{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/2876b8d3c2d6920da03a828ab411bb489bda9743cc0a210486c725348e14f13c.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x)y_1(x)+u_2(x)y_2(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2 y_2'.
$$

Here, $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_1 = \sin(4x), \qquad y_2 = \cos(4x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for $y_p,$ we get

$$
y_p =u_1\sin(4x)+u_2\cos(4x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for $y_p',$ we get

$$
y_p' = u_1(\sin(4x))'+u_2 (\cos(4x))'.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates $u_1'$ and $u_2'$ by differentiating $y_p$ and equating this expression to our constraint on $y_p'.$

Differentiating $y_p$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for $y_p',$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+\cancel{4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\cancel{4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)} & =\cancel{4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}-\cancel{4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
u_1' \sin(4x) + u_2' \cos(4x) = 0.
$$
